title: Industrial in-situ conversion of oil-shale kerogen

concept.text: The innovation is to convert kerogen—the organic material in oil-shale rock—into producible oil and gas while the rock remains underground, at a scale and duration suitable for an industrial operation. Heating causes the conversion. The intended capability combines subsurface heating, collection of the resulting fluids, measured positive usable-energy return and effective groundwater protection. A small conversion experiment demonstrates part of this capability; the full innovation requires these functions to work together over a commercial volume.

Shell’s In-situ Conversion Process at Mahogany provides a historical example of the approach. Shell reported small-scale production from heated oil shale and separately investigated groundwater exclusion using a freeze wall. PET-04 concerns the proposed industrial capability beyond that demonstration. Its scope excludes surface retorting, in which rock is excavated for conversion elsewhere, and does not assume that a successful heating experiment establishes commercial operation.

significance.text: The potential resource is exceptionally large. USGS Fact Sheet 2012–3145, published in January 2013, reports 4.285 trillion barrels of oil in place across the three principal Green River Formation basins in Colorado, Utah and Wyoming. Its grade-filtered totals include 1.146 trillion barrels in rock yielding at least 15 gallons per ton and 353 billion barrels at a cutoff of 25 gallons per ton. These are nested resource estimates at different grade thresholds, not quantities to add together and not demonstrated economically recoverable reserves.

Successful industrial conversion could make some of that kerogen resource producible without excavating the converted rock. The direct advance would be an integrated way to manufacture and recover hydrocarbon fluids underground from a solid organic resource. The scale of the in-place resource makes even a limited recoverable fraction potentially consequential, but neither its size nor its grade establishes achievable production rates, energy performance or an eventual industry’s size.

The distinction between resource abundance and usable supply is central. In 2011, USGS explained that it had not estimated economically recoverable oil because an economic recovery method had not yet been developed for Green River Formation oil shale. That statement describes conditions at publication. It supports the historical importance of the recovery problem but cannot establish its status in November 2026.

Conditional synthesis: if the technical milestone were achieved and subsequent economics were favorable, it could support additional petroleum supply and development of some kerogen-rich deposits. Positive net usable-energy return would still leave questions about capital cost, operating cost, water requirements, environmental effects and competitiveness. Avoiding excavation of the converted volume would not by itself establish a low-impact operation or widespread deployability.

missing_breakthrough.text: The capability sought is sustained conversion and recovery across a pre-defined commercial module, with positive measured net usable-energy return and effective fluid containment under the applicable permit. Shell’s January 2013 account explicitly distinguished small-scale technical success from the commercial proof still sought. The supplied historical evidence does not establish whether this integrated capability remains unavailable in November 2026.

Engineering synthesis: the scale-up problem is to deliver enough heat throughout the intended rock volume, sustain conversion, and recover the resulting fluids at a useful rate while controlling their movement. These functions must remain coordinated over years, including the operation of heating, pumping, processing and containment systems. Laboratory pyrolysis alone cannot establish field-scale heat delivery, fluid recovery or containment performance.

Groundwater control is a distinct engineering barrier. Shell investigated a freeze wall to exclude groundwater from the conversion area, showing that isolation was a separate development task alongside conversion. The supplied review does not establish complete containment performance across an industrial operation. It also provides no measured energy balance with which to determine whether heating, containment and production together yielded more usable energy than they consumed.

The earlier description of closely spaced electric production heaters, conduction-dominated heating, quantified slowness and high electricity demand is not established by the supplied evidence. The spacing identified in the review concerns freeze holes, not production heaters. Heat delivery and energy demand remain essential matters to measure, but this record cannot assign a production-heater geometry, heating timescale or energy penalty.

current_state.text: Shell’s Mahogany technology page, archived on 23 January 2013, reports that the Mahogany Demonstration Project South recovered 1,700 barrels of light oil plus associated gas from a 30-by-40-foot testing area. Shell characterized the process as technically successful at small scale, with commercial proof remaining. The reported oil volume is a cumulative recovery figure; the supplied account does not provide the production duration or complete energy accounting needed to infer a sustained industrial production rate or net energy return. No gas quantity is supplied here.

On 25 September 2013, Bill Lehane’s Upstream article reported Shell’s decision to end its Colorado Mahogany oil-shale research project after more than 15 years. The retained article opening supports that dated announcement. The supplied review found that the article text ends mid-sentence despite the extraction metadata indicating no truncation, so the available excerpt cannot support a fuller account of the decision or subsequent industry history.

The supplied evidence establishes historical small-scale conversion and an announced research-project termination. It contains no auditable bounded search results establishing subsequent Green River commercialization or the state of field methods as of November 2026. Consequently, neither the assertion that no in-situ industry followed nor a present-day pilot-scale ceiling can be concluded from this record. This evidence gap does not invalidate Shell’s dated demonstration or prove that later industrial success did or did not occur.

The resource and development evidence also have different access boundaries. According to the supplied review, the complete extracted text and table of the January 2013 USGS resource fact sheet support its numerical estimates; its figures were not inspected. The 2011 economic-method statement was available in a publication abstract, rather than the full four-page report. Shell’s retained webpage text appeared complete, but its referenced research chart was not supplied or inspected. These limitations constrain additional conclusions beyond the specific findings reported here.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration, not an established standard: define a commercial module before testing, including its rock volume, relevant geological conditions, conversion-temperature target, operating duration and minimum production rate. Demonstrate conversion and production for years at the declared rate, with operating interruptions and recovery totals reported. The supplied record does not justify numerical thresholds for module size, temperature, duration or rate. Shell’s 30-by-40-foot demonstration would not satisfy the proposed industrial-scale criterion by itself.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed demonstration, not an established standard

completion_criteria.text: Proposed energy test: measure the usable energy in recovered products and all material energy inputs over a declared accounting boundary and period. Include heating, containment, pumping and processing, and disclose how construction, startup, shutdown and externally supplied utilities are treated. Demonstrate positive net usable-energy return with uncertainty reported. A result based only on heater input or gross oil output would leave the integrated energy requirement unresolved.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed energy test

completion_criteria.text: Proposed containment test: verify groundwater performance against the host regulator’s permit and independently assess fluid movement around the conversion volume. Declare monitoring locations, relevant substances, detection limits, baseline conditions and the observation period, including an appropriate period after heating and production end. Permit compliance would be necessary under this proposal, but would not alone establish comprehensive containment beyond the permit’s measured scope.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed containment test

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: make the operating methods, production records, energy accounting and environmental measurements available for independent assessment, and repeat the result in additional modules or relevant geological settings. Such demonstrations would establish performance across the tested conditions, not universal applicability to oil shale. Meeting the technical criteria would still require a separate assessment of profitability and practical deployment constraints.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison: PET-05, “Shale-oil recovery from the matrix,” shares a focus on obtaining oil from shale-related rock. PET-04 specifically requires conversion of kerogen into fluids underground; PET-05’s title identifies recovery from the matrix as its target. These remain separate capabilities. The supplied record does not provide a detailed PET-05 definition or evidence supporting a broader comparison with tight-oil production.

Roster-based comparison: PET-09, “Bitumen that flows at native reservoir temperature,” targets bitumen mobility, while PET-11, “In-reservoir conversion of bitumen to pipeline-specification crude,” targets conversion to a specified product quality. PET-04 instead targets conversion of kerogen-bearing oil shale at industrial scale. It shares subsurface production challenges with PET-09 and conversion challenges with PET-11, but does not inherit either concept’s feedstock, native-temperature condition or pipeline-quality endpoint. These distinctions follow from the supplied concept titles; no additional comparative performance claims are established.

Roster-based comparison: PET-03, “Commercial gas production from methane hydrate,” likewise concerns making a subsurface resource commercially producible, but addresses a different material and product. PET-06, “Hydrogen from petroleum reservoirs, with the other products left underground,” shares an underground-conversion theme while specifying hydrogen recovery and retention of other products. PET-04 seeks production of oil and gas from kerogen and does not imply the product-retention capability of PET-06.

Roster-based comparison: PET-01, “Blind prediction of multiphase reservoir flow,” and PET-08, “Permeability and saturation measured through the reservoir volume,” concern prediction and measurement that could help assess fluid recovery and containment in an in-situ conversion project. PET-02, “Conventional-oil recovery at gas-field recovery factors,” concerns recovery of an existing conventional-oil resource. Success in any of these would not alone establish PET-04’s heating, conversion, energy or industrial-operation requirements.

Roster-based comparison: PET-07, “Deep well construction without a steep depth penalty,” could affect the practicality of accessing and instrumenting subsurface operations. PET-10, “A pressure plan with a prospectively tested earthquake bound,” concerns a separate operational risk capability wherever pressure management is relevant. PET-04 does not establish either economical deep-well construction or a tested earthquake bound, and the supplied record does not establish how strongly either capability would constrain a particular conversion project.

Scope distinction: surface retorting is outside PET-04 because its conversion step occurs after excavation. The earlier reference to commercial Estonian kukersite practice is not retained as an established comparison: the supplied evidence does not document that practice. This evidentiary limit does not alter the distinction between surface processing and the in-situ capability defined here.

change_log.change: Preserved PET-04’s identity and integrated its conversion, energy, containment and industrial-operation requirements into a single concept.
change_log.reason: The useful innovation is an integrated field capability; neither laboratory conversion nor one unsupported supporting assertion determines the validity of the whole concept.

change_log.change: Replaced asserted production-heater spacing, conduction dominance, slowness and electricity intensity with explicit evidence limits.
change_log.reason: The supplied review supports heating-induced conversion but does not establish those particulars; the documented spacing concerns freeze holes.

change_log.change: Retained the 1,700-barrel result, associated gas and 30-by-40-foot area while separating cumulative recovery from production rate and energy performance.
change_log.reason: The historical demonstration is supported, but the supplied evidence does not provide the duration, gas quantity or complete energy balance needed for stronger conclusions.

change_log.change: Dated the Mahogany termination announcement and disclosed the partial Upstream extraction.
change_log.reason: The retained opening supports the September 2013 decision but cannot establish a complete project history or later developments.

change_log.change: Removed categorical claims that no Green River in-situ industry followed and that current methods remain pilot-scale.
change_log.reason: The supplied freshness record contains no auditable search results establishing those present-day or industry-wide conclusions.

change_log.change: Preserved all supported USGS quantities and assigned the 15- and 25-gallon-per-ton cutoffs to their corresponding resource totals.
change_log.reason: The totals describe nested grade-filtered in-place resources, not additive volumes, economic reserves or demonstrated recoverable fractions.

change_log.change: Kept the 2011 economic-recovery statement explicitly historical and preserved its abstract-only access boundary.
change_log.reason: The statement supports the historical development problem without establishing conditions in 2026.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed demonstration to include declared scale and operating targets, full energy boundaries, containment monitoring and independent reproducibility.
change_log.reason: These details make the proposed milestone assessable while distinguishing technical success from profitability and finite demonstrations from universal applicability.

change_log.change: Retained roster-based distinctions with PET-09 and PET-11 and added relationships to the other supplied concepts, with unsupported comparisons labeled as synthesis.
change_log.reason: The roster supports distinctions between the named targets even though the historical sources do not document comparative performance. The unsupported Estonian commercial-practice assertion was omitted.

change_log.change: Preserved source-access limitations for the USGS figures, 2011 report, Shell chart and Upstream excerpt.
change_log.reason: The final record must not imply inspection beyond the supplied review or treat incomplete evidence as proof that a result is false.

unresolved_issues: Whether any later Green River project demonstrated sustained industrial in-situ conversion by November 2026 remains unestablished in the supplied record.
The supplied Mahogany evidence does not resolve production duration, associated-gas quantity, complete energy inputs, net usable-energy return or industrial containment performance.

Commercial-module size, conversion temperature, multi-year duration, production targets, energy-accounting conventions and post-operation monitoring periods remain to be specified for a convincing demonstration.
The economically recoverable fraction, commercial competitiveness and practical deployment scale cannot be inferred from the USGS in-place resource estimates.

The original review recommended removing the PET-09/PET-11 comparisons from the evidence-backed significance claim. Their unsupported empirical form was removed, but conceptual distinctions were retained under related_concepts because the supplied roster explicitly identifies the different targets.
The supplied record does not establish commercial Estonian kukersite practice; that factual comparison remains unresolved and is not used to support PET-04.
